question: Defined by behaviour rather than by a shared backbone, a _____ is any of the water-shunning molecules a cell uses to store energy, build its membranes and carry signals.
questions: A gram of fat yields more than twice the energy a gram of carbohydrate does, which is why an animal that must carry its reserves banks them in _____ form rather than sugar.
Mass-spectrometry surveys find more than a thousand distinct _____ species in a single mammalian cell, and nobody yet knows why a cell should need so many.
abstract:
Lipids are a diverse group of small molecules, hydrophobic or amphipathic, whose chemical structures vary widely, so the category is held together by how its members behave in water rather than by a common backbone. The simplest are the fatty acids, long hydrocarbon chains ending in a carboxyl group, whose nonpolar carbon-hydrogen bonds cannot interact with water; that hydrophobicity governs much of how the more complex lipids behave. Cells put them to three uses: storing energy, building membranes and carrying signals. Fats, three fatty acids joined to a glycerol, are the storage form, and they yield more than twice as much energy per unit weight as carbohydrates, which lets an animal hold the same reserve in less than half the body weight. Phospholipids, two fatty acids attached to a polar head group, are the principal components of cell membranes.

That tidy list understates the category, because a single cell type can hold hundreds to thousands of distinct lipid species, and mammalian cells more than a thousand, differing in head group, chain length and degree of unsaturation. Why a cell should maintain so many is unsettled, and the explanations on offer run from the physics of membranes through specific binding to proteins to signalling and evolutionary history. Part of the answer is that the mixture is tuned rather than fixed: cold packs membrane lipids more tightly, so organisms vary the proportion carrying unsaturated chains to hold fluidity steady, a response called homeoviscous adaptation. Escherichia coli completes it within a single generation of a temperature shock, using a valve that shunts synthesis between the saturated and unsaturated branches and a feedback loop that deliberately overshoots before settling. How much of the variety is strictly necessary is another open question, since a synthetic compartment can be made from a single lipid species and how complex a lipidome a self-reproducing cell needs is not known.
